newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - On Buy Nothing Day, try curbing the urge to shop.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - On Buy Nothing Day, try curbing the urge to shop.

text.p: Fed up with over-the-top commercialization of Christmas? Here's a novel way to mark the beginning of the holiday shopping season: for just one day, buy absolutely nothing.

"Buy Nothing Day," organized by a loose coalition of international groups, will be held on Nov. 29, the day after America's Thanksgiving and the unofficial start of the Christmas and Chanukah gift-buying rush. It is usually one of the busiest shopping days of the year.

"The concept is a 24-hour moratorium on consumer spending. It's a very personal pledge to go on a consumer fast for one day to find out what it's like to curb the impulse to buy," said Kalle Lasn, director of the Vancouver-based Media Foundation, one of the event's backers.

They may be barely noticeable among the hordes of shoppers, but Buy Nothing Day's organizers hope more than 100,000 people in the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Britain, South Africa, Japan, Sweden and Belgium will fight off the urge to buy.

Started by a Canadian group five years ago, the day aims to draw attention to overconsumption and its environmental and social consequences. Organizers hope to awaken shoppers to the "joys of buying less and living more simply with less environmental damage, less stress, more happiness and personal fulfillment."
"People who try it gain an awareness about their lifestyle and our consumer culture that encourages us to buy, buy, buy. Buying is like an addiction for us in the West," Lasn said.

Organizers, a collection of grassroots community groups and foundations in 10 countries, do not seriously expect to make a dent in retailers' sales that day. Nor are they trying to convince people to quit shopping altogether. Rather, they hope to spark awareness and debate.

"It's a great opportunity to raise consciousness about how our buying habits affect us, our environment, our souls," said Betsy Taylor of the Maryland-based Center for a New American Dream, which is exploring ways to redefine cultural values.

"It's a way of making people aware there are better ways to spend time than strolling through shopping malls. We are so focused on material things as a source of fulfillment we have lost touch with the fact that non-material things are the true source of happiness."

Supporters plan to mark the day with a variety of events. Taylor and a group of friends will gather for a sing-along, the type of non-commercialized fun that she said has largely been lost amid the rush to buy. At Kestrel Books in Vancouver, owner Ron Fryer said he will try to dissuade customers from buying that day, although he does not plan to close his doors.

A coalition of Nebraska churches has endorsed the day and written to 22 newspapers promoting it. In Albuquerque, New Mexico, students at Freedom High School are signing a pledge to buy nothing on Nov. 29. In Missoula, Montana, a demonstration is planned at a local shopping mall. And in Seattle, Buy Nothing Day supporters plan to cut up credit cards and sponsor street theater about overconsumption.

Buy Nothing Day is gaining more attention this year than in the past partly because it was switched from September to the more strategic pre-Christmas date, supporters said. But it also dovetails with another emerging movement dubbed "voluntary simplicity" in which many once-avid consumers reject materialism and pare down their lifestyles. All this plays to a society where corporate layoffs and economic uncertainty have prompted a reexamination of values.

"Buy Nothing Day has growing momentum," Richard Celente, president of the New York-based Trends Research Institute, said. It is striking a chord among "people who are cutting back and finding more joy in not spending." His group estimates about five percent of the 76 million baby boomers in the United States have embraced this new simplicity and says this will rise to 15 percent by 2000.

Not surprisingly, advertisers and retailers are cool to the idea of Buy Nothing Day. The three major U.S. television networks rejected the Media Foundation's Buy Nothing Day ad in which a cartoon pig superimposed on a map of the United States urges consumers to "give it a rest" for the day.
NBC called the spot hostile to advertisers' interests and said consumers want traditional advertising. But CNN agreed to run the ad, the Media Foundation said.
The International Council of Shopping Centers, a trade group for malls, dismissed the day as "a political stunt."
"We think it's misguided. They are losing sight of the millions of people employed in shopping centers and the economic impact," spokesman Mark Schoifet said.
